Reading crisis

By: Viewfinder | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche we investigate how government inaction is driving the illiteracy crisis

Unique Selling Point:
Our story of “accountability failure” hinges showing that the Provinces and Department of Basic Education has done very little to plan, budget or implement literacy programmes in spite of the President and the Department’s commitment to the 2030 goal that all kids should be able to read for meaning by 2030. Through records requests I have secured a copy of what the Department touts as its “National Reading Plan” - in reality this document is just a table of “activities” and “targets”. Access to this document is exclusive and significant, because even education sector experts have never seen it, and have been calling for its release. Analysing it shows that it is actually not an implementable plan, because it has no delegation of responsibilities, means for measuring progress towards targets or budgets for executing activities associated with it. We have now submitted further records requests for the department to provide us with the monitoring and evaluation reports to show what - if any - progress has been made. I have some ideas for how to build outrage in narration and graphics in support of this point.

Summary:
Executive summary
Being able to read is one of the most important ways for a child to break out of a cycle of intergenerational poverty. As many as 80 percent of Grade 4 children in SA cannot read. Despite the president and government’s commitment that every Grade 4 child should be able to read for meaning by 2030, SA’s children are making pitifully slow progress towards this goal.

Using the findings of the Reading Panel 2030’s recent report on government’s progress, we have identified that the lack of planning, implementable literacy programs and budgets at both the national and provincial departmental levels is an important driver of the literacy crisis in South Africa.

We have gained access - through permission from a principle - to a school in a township outside Makhanda in the Eastern Cape. With this and other access in Makhanda, we will be able to report the literacy crisis via educators and activists working at the coalface.

We have also identified experts to interview and started a right-of-reply engagements with the national and provincial education departments - asking them to respond to the finding of lacking plans, programs and budgets for improved reading outcomes.

Overview: Government failures are driving the literacy crisis in South Africa
Being able to read is one of the most important determinants for children to break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. In 2014, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation published findings that if all students in low income countries left school with basic reading skills, 171 million people could be lifted out of extreme poverty, equivalent to a 12% reduction in the world total (UNESCO, 2014).

In his 2019 State of the Nation Address, President Cyril Ramaphosa said that reading comprehension for children was “possibly the single most important factor in overcoming poverty, unemployment and inequality”. And, in his first State of the Nation Address after being re-elected later that year, the President reiterated the need to “mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign” towards the goal of ensuring that every 10-year-old will be able to read by 2030.

The President’s comments came against a backdrop of a steady improvement in the percentage of children who could read in recent years (Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) trends for SA 2006, 2011, 2016). But, these gains have been very slow. At this trajectory it would take more than 80 years to reach government’s goal. And, though there have been improvements. The most recent results from leading international study for figures show that nearly 80 percent of grade 4 children could not read in 2016, placing South Africa way behind reading outcomes in much poorer countries such as Kenya and Swaziland.

The results for the 2021 edition of the PILRS are not out yet, but projections are not good. If learning losses due to the Covid-19 are taken into account, experts project that fewer children can read today than was the case before the pandemic.

A panel of civil society leaders and education experts was convened in 2022 by Dr. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, the former United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women, to monitor South Africa’s progress towards the 2030 goal. The Reading Panel 2030’s latest report, published in February, has concluded that failures within government are also important drivers of the literacy crisis in South Africa.

Though Basic Education Minister Angie Motshekga has stated her Department’s commitment to realising the President’s 2030 literacy goal. The Department’s plans have been vague, and its budget allocations negligible.

Last year, the Department’s Director General Hubert Mweli told Parliament that a “National Reading Plan” was being implemented by all Provincial Education Departments and a number of other “line functions” within the Department.

But, experts on the Reading Panel 2030 have noted that the National Reading Plan had not been published, throwing doubt on whether it even exists

We queried the Department, and filed records requests for a copy of the reading plan and the minutes of progress meetings touted by the Department of Parliament last year. To date, DBE’s spokesperson Elijah Mhlanga has not responded and our records request is pending.

In last year’s budget vote, the Minister reiterated the importance of “improving reading in the early grades”. But, the only budget line item dedicated to reading for Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) had been allocated R11.1 million, amounting to well below 1 percent of the Department’s annual budget.

The DBE’s Primary School Reading Improvement Program (PSRIP) also draws a relatively small budget and its goals and interventions, the panel have concluded, fall well short of what is needed. The lack of a budget for reading is not because the budget is not nuanced. A number of other Department specific priority areas have been allocated conditional grants to which are disbursed directly to provinces, there is no such grant for reading.

Indeed, the bulk of the education sector’s budget is spent at the level of provincial departments of education, which run schools and employ teachers. The Reading Panel concluded that most provincial departments have also not planned, developed programs or allocated budgets specifically for improved reading outcomes.

Also, a major shortcoming hampering the effective teaching of reading is that teachers and classrooms are not equipped with the physical materials and resources that are needed. In his 2019 SONA, President Ramaphosa said that “[Government] will be substantially expanding the availability of these early reading resources across the foundation phase of schooling”. In 2008, the Department published a list of ten minimum resources needed for literacy teaching, but only DBE “workbooks”, leaving a massive resource gap.

Field reporting from the coalface of the literacy crisis
Further to this high-level picture, this story will be produced on the ground in the Eastern Cape - the country’s poorest province with a history of poor basic education outcomes .

Provincial education departments: We have submitted queries to each provincial education department asking them to outline what reading interventions and budgets they have in place, and to respond to the Reading Panel 2030 finding that there are no such funded programs at the provincial level, except programs in the Western Cape and Gauteng.

Press Release:


Teaching children to read is fundamental to their future success. But for a country already battling massive youth unemployment and an adult literacy crisis, it’s emerged that close to 80 per cent of grade 4 learners cannot read with understanding in any of the eleven official languages. Government was warned of the crisis and, in 2019, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised to prioritise reading through a National Reading Plan. But, through exclusive access, Carte Blanche shows how Department of Education documents reveal a plan in disarray, continuing to fail our children. Despite this, education officials continue to proclaim the National Reading Plan a success. Carte Blanche investigates.

Script:


Voice
It is the first week of term and ten-year-old Lilitha Marangxa is getting ready for school. Lilitha lives with her mother and grandmother in Tantyi township in Makhanda in the Eastern Cape. A supportive home environment and access to a school where teachers are able to give their learners one-on-one attention has meant that Lilitha is an extreme outlier in South Africa: a Gr 4 learner who is reading at a level much higher than expected for her age.

Claire
Ah, so this is your reading corner.

Lilitha Marangxa
This is the shelf where I keep my books. This is where I sit. This is where I put my bag. And these are the books.

Claire
So do you have favourite books that you like to read?

Lilitha
Yes. This one.

Claire
Do you love reading that one?

Lilitha
Yes… Gina woke up the next morning to find the sun shining through her bedroom curtains. Birdsong twittered from the nearby trees, but it was so early that she couldn't hear any cars going past on the road outside.

Claire
Why do you think you're so good with reading?

Lilitha
I think it's because when I was in grade R I started looking at picture books and then I saw books with like actual words. Then my mom helped me read those words.

Voice
But, the majority of children of Lilitha’s age and background are falling far behind. Makhanda IN THE EASTERN CAPE is a microcosm of South Africa’s unequal education system. Here are some of the country’s most exclusive schools, and a top university. But, it is also a place of deprivation and a community at the forefront of one of the country’s most under-recognised crises. The majority of young children here cannot read. They are not alone.

In 2016, 78 percent of South Africa’s Gr 4’s could not read for meaning in any language.

Across the way from Lilitha’s home, Grade 3s at Tantyi Primary are revising their English
reading lessons. Many struggle to keep up.

Due to a staff shortage, Ms Mandisa Peter is Tantyi Primary’s only teacher for Grade 2 and
Grade 3. She has fifty-eight children who rely on her almost exclusively for reading
instruction.

Claire Mawisa
What does it feel like when you meet a child who cannot read?

Mandisa Peter
You feel so sad and frustrated because it reflects what is happening in class [...] Because, you know, there's an ability to that child. It's just that she or he didn't get that one-on-one support.

Cyril Ramaphosa
Another critical priority is to substantially improve reading comprehension in the first years of school […] It is possibly the single most important factor in overcoming poverty, unemployment and inequality.

Cyril Ramaphosa
If we are to ensure that within the next decade, every 10-year-old will be able to read for
meaning, we will need to mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign.

Voice
Rampahosa made this one of five fundamental goals for his term in office. But, four years later, education experts agree that there is no “massive reading campaign” underway in the country.

Though other priority areas of the Department of Basic Education are well-funded. Minister Angie Motshekga has allocated virtually no budget to improving reading outcomes.

Despite that red flag, Motshekga’s Director General told Parliament last year that a “National Reading Plan was implemented by all provinces”. But this secretive plan has never been published and progress towards its supposed implementation has never been made available for public scrutiny.

Whatever the Department is doing, it is evidently not enough.

With learning losses due to Covid-19, it is projected that a higher percentage of children cannot read today, compared to when the President made his grand commitment in 2019.

Link
Teachers at schools like Tantyi Primary in Makhanda are at the coalface of the reading crisis in South Africa. They are still waiting for the support promised by the president more than four years ago. And it is their learners - whose only hope of escaping poverty is learning to read - who are left behind.

Voice
Professor Nic Spaull is an Education Economist at Stellenbosch University and a member of the Reading Panel 2030, a civil society organisation set up to monitor progress towards the president’s goal.

Claire
Sitting here in 2023. Would you classify this as a crisis and if so, why?

Nic Spaull
The fact that 78% of grade four children cannot read for meaning in any language, all 11 languages were assessed. If that's not a crisis, I don't know what a crisis is… And obviously if you don't have a plan and you don't have a budget, there's not going to be any progress. And then are we really surprised by why children drop out, why we have such high levels of youth unemployment. It's not a surprise to me.

Noncedo Madubedube is the General Secretary of Equal Education and another member of the Reading Panel.

Claire
Give us the bigger picture if things don't change.

Noncedo Madubedube
If we've got the vast majority of learners in the education system in no fee-paying schools, unable to comprehend words - read for meaning, think for themselves - it means that we lose innovation, creativity, critical analysis that lends itself to a massive skills deficit in South Africa's near future.

Voice
But, that scenario is already a reality. A lack of “reading comprehension” tops the list of skill shortages in South Africa’s labour market.

Claire
What has the Department of Basic Education done to implement reading programs?

Noncedo
[...] The Department of Basic Education, both at the national and the provincial level, aren't doing enough to put in place an adequate plan - something that's comprehensive and measurable - that can make sure that we can evaluate and see improvements in evaluation improvements outcomes in learning in schools through reading.

The department has absolutely failed in this regard. And also, to me, it feels shameless around its failures.

Now, a public records request by investigative newsrooms Viewfinder and GroundUp has unearthed for the first time what the Department claims as its National Reading Plan. This plan is in fact not a plan at all. It is just a long table with a list of forty seven activities. Some, like improved reading resources in classrooms, are desperately needed interventions. Most, however, are so abstract as to border on the absurd: such encouraging food companies to follow the Chappies bubblegum example of putting reading materials in their packaging.

But, who is tasked and accountable? How are these activities to be funded? How is progress supposed to be monitored? Those questions are all left unanswered.

Link
The Department of Basic Education has claimed in Parliament that it and the nine provinces are implementing a National Reading Plan. But, our exclusive access to this document has exposed a huge disconnect with what is really happening in schools on the ground.

Nic
Well, first of all, thanks Carte Blanche for getting it. None of us had access to this plan. We didn't actually know that it existed [...] It's still not in the public domain. There is still no budget for it. There is still no reporting against it.

I do think it's a wish list.

Voice
When we accessed the provincial progress reports for this plan, the Department asked us not to share these publicly, to protect certain officials’ identities. And we are not surprised.

These reports show that the plan’s implementation is a random, uncoordinated mess. While some provinces, like the Western Cape, appear to be doing their best to fund and implement localised reading plans, others like Limpopo, appear to be doing almost nothing.

Voice
Dr Stephen Taylor is the Department’s head of monitoring and implementation.

Claire
Stephen, from the plan that we have that is not public, it is not a proper plan.

Claire
Do you think that the Department of Basic Education is doing enough to make sure that we
meet the President's goals of 2030 to make sure that children are reading for meaning?

Stephen Taylor
Well I think it would be very unfair to call the existing plan and the weaknesses and the implementation against the existing plan an abject failure because of the timing of this plan. As I've said, this plan was something that was approved just before the pandemic set in, and we had to respond to the priorities caused by the pandemic.

Claire
I think what we perhaps wanted was what is the Department of Basic Education going to do from now on?

Stephen
Yes. So I think a new revised plan that we're working on. It needs to succeed in bringing better coordination to the sector.

[transition back to Classroom]
For teachers like Mandisa Peters, one need stands out amongst all others. She is completely overwhelmed by the sheer number of children looking up to her. In South Africa, the ratio of teachers-to-learners is ever worsening, and with a looming retirement crisis in the sector, the situation is only expected to get worse.

Claire
What type of support do you need as a teacher in this phase of learning?.

Mandisa
They must give us teachers. They must give us teachers to assist these learners.

Claire
A message that you'd like to say deliver to the Department of Basic Education. What would that message be, if you had the opportunity?

Nic
I think I would tell the minister that essentially we need to move away from slogans and words and aspirations to budgets and actions. The time for talk is over. The time for saying we're going to do things is over. You need to act. You need to allocate budget and you need to act.

Claire
What will happen to all of your beautiful children in your class if they didn't grasp how to read
with understanding […] What would the future look like?

Ms Peter
Their future, it’s not going to be good [...] it's not going to be good seeing them in future not going that far because you failed them, not giving them all that you can give because you are one. And there's a lot that is looking from you.

Promo 1 (11 seconds)
Illiteracy is a crisis in South Africa. But with no plan in place, and virtually no budget allocated to reading programs, is it any wonder that the majority of our children cannot read.

Promo 2 (21 seconds)
As many as 80 percent of ten-year-olds in South Africa cannot read. We visit a school at the coal face of this crisis, and ask a teacher here why it persists, when President Ramaphosa has committed to eradicate illiteracy by the end of the decade.

Promo 3 (21 seconds)
Improved literacy is a major priority of the Ramaphosa Presidency.
Ramaphosa: we will need to mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign.
But, our exclusive access to the Department of Basic Education’s planning documents shows why there has been no progress.
Noncedo: “The department has absolutely failed in this regard. And also, to me, it feels shameless around its failures.

Lilitha lives with her mother and grandmother in Tantyi township in Makhanda in the Eastern Cape. A supportive home environment and access to a school where teachers are able to give their learners one-on-one attention has meant that Lilitha is an extreme outlier in South Africa: a Gr 4 learner who is reading at a level much higher than expected for her age. Claire Ah, so this is your reading corner. Lilitha Marangxa This is the shelf where I keep my books. This is where I sit. This is where I put my bag. And these are the books. Claire So do you have favourite books that you like to read? Lilitha Yes. This one. Claire Do you love reading that one? Lilitha Yes… Gina woke up the next morning to find the sun shining through her bedroom curtains. Birdsong twittered from the nearby trees, but it was so early that she couldn't hear any cars going past on the road outside. Claire Why do you think you're so good with reading? Lilitha I think it's because when I was in grade R I started looking at picture books and then I saw books with like actual words. Then my mom helped me read those words. Voice But, the majority of children of Lilitha’s age and background are falling far behind. Makhanda IN THE EASTERN CAPE is a microcosm of South Africa’s unequal education system. Here are some of the country’s most exclusive schools, and a top university. But, it is also a place of deprivation and a community at the forefront of one of the country’s most under-recognised crises. The majority of young children here cannot read. They are not alone. In 2016, 78 percent of South Africa’s Gr 4’s could not read for meaning in any language. Across the way from Lilitha’s home, Grade 3s at Tantyi Primary are revising their English reading lessons. Many struggle to keep up. Due to a staff shortage, Ms Mandisa Peter is Tantyi Primary’s only teacher for Grade 2 and Grade 3. She has fifty-eight children who rely on her almost exclusively for reading instruction. Claire Mawisa What does it feel like when you meet a child who cannot read? Mandisa Peter You feel so sad and frustrated because it reflects what is happening in class [...] Because, you know, there's an ability to that child. It's just that she or he didn't get that one-on-one support. Cyril Ramaphosa Another critical priority is to substantially improve reading comprehension in the first years of school […] It is possibly the single most important factor in overcoming poverty, unemployment and inequality. Cyril Ramaphosa If we are to ensure that within the next decade, every 10-year-old will be able to read for meaning, we will need to mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign. Voice Rampahosa made this one of five fundamental goals for his term in office. But, four years later, education experts agree that there is no “massive reading campaign” underway in the country. Though other priority areas of the Department of Basic Education are well-funded. Minister Angie Motshekga has allocated virtually no budget to improving reading outcomes. Despite that red flag, Motshekga’s Director General told Parliament last year that a “National Reading Plan was implemented by all provinces”. But this secretive plan has never been published and progress towards its supposed implementation has never been made available for public scrutiny. Whatever the Department is doing, it is evidently not enough. With learning losses due to Covid-19, it is projected that a higher percentage of children cannot read today, compared to when the President made his grand commitment in 2019. Link Teachers at schools like Tantyi Primary in Makhanda are at the coalface of the reading crisis in South Africa. They are still waiting for the support promised by the president more than four years ago. And it is their learners - whose only hope of escaping poverty is learning to read - who are left behind. Voice Professor Nic Spaull is an Education Economist at Stellenbosch University and a member of the Reading Panel 2030, a civil society organisation set up to monitor progress towards the president’s goal. Claire Sitting here in 2023. Would you classify this as a crisis and if so, why? Nic Spaull The fact that 78% of grade four children cannot read for meaning in any language, all 11 languages were assessed. If that's not a crisis, I don't know what a crisis is… And obviously if you don't have a plan and you don't have a budget, there's not going to be any progress. And then are we really surprised by why children drop out, why we have such high levels of youth unemployment. It's not a surprise to me. Noncedo Madubedube is the General Secretary of Equal Education and another member of the Reading Panel. Claire Give us the bigger picture if things don't change. Noncedo Madubedube If we've got the vast majority of learners in the education system in no fee-paying schools, unable to comprehend words - read for meaning, think for themselves - it means that we lose innovation, creativity, critical analysis that lends itself to a massive skills deficit in South Africa's near future. Voice But, that scenario is already a reality. A lack of “reading comprehension” tops the list of skill shortages in South Africa’s labour market. Claire What has the Department of Basic Education done to implement reading programs? Noncedo [...] The Department of Basic Education, both at the national and the provincial level, aren't doing enough to put in place an adequate plan - something that's comprehensive and measurable - that can make sure that we can evaluate and see improvements in evaluation improvements outcomes in learning in schools through reading. The department has absolutely failed in this regard. And also, to me, it feels shameless around its failures. Now, a public records request by investigative newsrooms Viewfinder and GroundUp has unearthed for the first time what the Department claims as its National Reading Plan. This plan is in fact not a plan at all. It is just a long table with a list of forty seven activities. Some, like improved reading resources in classrooms, are desperately needed interventions. Most, however, are so abstract as to border on the absurd: such encouraging food companies to follow the Chappies bubblegum example of putting reading materials in their packaging. But, who is tasked and accountable? How are these activities to be funded? How is progress supposed to be monitored? Those questions are all left unanswered. Link The Department of Basic Education has claimed in Parliament that it and the nine provinces are implementing a National Reading Plan. But, our exclusive access to this document has exposed a huge disconnect with what is really happening in schools on the ground. Nic Well, first of all, thanks Carte Blanche for getting it. None of us had access to this plan. We didn't actually know that it existed [...] It's still not in the public domain. There is still no budget for it. There is still no reporting against it. I do think it's a wish list. Voice When we accessed the provincial progress reports for this plan, the Department asked us not to share these publicly, to protect certain officials’ identities. And we are not surprised. These reports show that the plan’s implementation is a random, uncoordinated mess. While some provinces, like the Western Cape, appear to be doing their best to fund and implement localised reading plans, others like Limpopo, appear to be doing almost nothing. Voice Dr Stephen Taylor is the Department’s head of monitoring and implementation. Claire Stephen, from the plan that we have that is not public, it is not a proper plan. Claire Do you think that the Department of Basic Education is doing enough to make sure that we meet the President's goals of 2030 to make sure that children are reading for meaning? Stephen Taylor Well I think it would be very unfair to call the existing plan and the weaknesses and the implementation against the existing plan an abject failure because of the timing of this plan. As I've said, this plan was something that was approved just before the pandemic set in, and we had to respond to the priorities caused by the pandemic. Claire I think what we perhaps wanted was what is the Department of Basic Education going to do from now on? Stephen Yes. So I think a new revised plan that we're working on. It needs to succeed in bringing better coordination to the sector. [transition back to Classroom] For teachers like Mandisa Peters, one need stands out amongst all others. She is completely overwhelmed by the sheer number of children looking up to her. In South Africa, the ratio of teachers-to-learners is ever worsening, and with a looming retirement crisis in the sector, the situation is only expected to get worse. Claire What type of support do you need as a teacher in this phase of learning?. Mandisa They must give us teachers. They must give us teachers to assist these learners. Claire A message that you'd like to say deliver to the Department of Basic Education. What would that message be, if you had the opportunity? Nic I think I would tell the minister that essentially we need to move away from slogans and words and aspirations to budgets and actions. The time for talk is over. The time for saying we're going to do things is over. You need to act. You need to allocate budget and you need to act. Claire What will happen to all of your beautiful children in your class if they didn't grasp how to read with understanding […] What would the future look like? Ms Peter Their future, it’s not going to be good [...] it's not going to be good seeing them in future not going that far because you failed them, not giving them all that you can give because you are one. And there's a lot that is looking from you. Promo 1 (11 seconds) Illiteracy is a crisis in South Africa. But with no plan in place, and virtually no budget allocated to reading programs, is it any wonder that the majority of our children cannot read. Promo 2 (21 seconds) As many as 80 percent of ten-year-olds in South Africa cannot read. We visit a school at the coal face of this crisis, and ask a teacher here why it persists, when President Ramaphosa has committed to eradicate illiteracy by the end of the decade. Promo 3 (21 seconds) Improved literacy is a major priority of the Ramaphosa Presidency. Ramaphosa: we will need to mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign. But, our exclusive access to the Department of Basic Education’s planning documents shows why there has been no progress. Noncedo: “The department has absolutely failed in this regard. And also, to me, it feels shameless around its failures.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche we investigate how government inaction is driving the illiteracy crisis
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Our story of “accountability failure” hinges showing that the Provinces and Department of Basic Education has done very little to plan, budget or implement literacy programmes in spite of the President and the Department’s commitment to the 2030 goal that all kids should be able to read for meaning by 2030. Through records requests I have secured a copy of what the Department touts as its “National Reading Plan” - in reality this document is just a table of “activities” and “targets”. Access to this document is exclusive and significant, because even education sector experts have never seen it, and have been calling for its release. Analysing it shows that it is actually not an implementable plan, because it has no delegation of responsibilities, means for measuring progress towards targets or budgets for executing activities associated with it. We have now submitted further records requests for the department to provide us with the monitoring and evaluation reports to show what - if any - progress has been made. I have some ideas for how to build outrage in narration and graphics in support of this point.
metadata.Summary: Executive summary Being able to read is one of the most important ways for a child to break out of a cycle of intergenerational poverty. As many as 80 percent of Grade 4 children in SA cannot read. Despite the president and government’s commitment that every Grade 4 child should be able to read for meaning by 2030, SA’s children are making pitifully slow progress towards this goal. Using the findings of the Reading Panel 2030’s recent report on government’s progress, we have identified that the lack of planning, implementable literacy programs and budgets at both the national and provincial departmental levels is an important driver of the literacy crisis in South Africa. We have gained access - through permission from a principle - to a school in a township outside Makhanda in the Eastern Cape. With this and other access in Makhanda, we will be able to report the literacy crisis via educators and activists working at the coalface. We have also identified experts to interview and started a right-of-reply engagements with the national and provincial education departments - asking them to respond to the finding of lacking plans, programs and budgets for improved reading outcomes. Overview: Government failures are driving the literacy crisis in South Africa Being able to read is one of the most important determinants for children to break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. In 2014, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation published findings that if all students in low income countries left school with basic reading skills, 171 million people could be lifted out of extreme poverty, equivalent to a 12% reduction in the world total (UNESCO, 2014). In his 2019 State of the Nation Address, President Cyril Ramaphosa said that reading comprehension for children was “possibly the single most important factor in overcoming poverty, unemployment and inequality”. And, in his first State of the Nation Address after being re-elected later that year, the President reiterated the need to “mobilise the entire nation behind a massive reading campaign” towards the goal of ensuring that every 10-year-old will be able to read by 2030. The President’s comments came against a backdrop of a steady improvement in the percentage of children who could read in recent years (Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) trends for SA 2006, 2011, 2016). But, these gains have been very slow. At this trajectory it would take more than 80 years to reach government’s goal. And, though there have been improvements. The most recent results from leading international study for figures show that nearly 80 percent of grade 4 children could not read in 2016, placing South Africa way behind reading outcomes in much poorer countries such as Kenya and Swaziland. The results for the 2021 edition of the PILRS are not out yet, but projections are not good. If learning losses due to the Covid-19 are taken into account, experts project that fewer children can read today than was the case before the pandemic. A panel of civil society leaders and education experts was convened in 2022 by Dr. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, the former United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women, to monitor South Africa’s progress towards the 2030 goal. The Reading Panel 2030’s latest report, published in February, has concluded that failures within government are also important drivers of the literacy crisis in South Africa. Though Basic Education Minister Angie Motshekga has stated her Department’s commitment to realising the President’s 2030 literacy goal. The Department’s plans have been vague, and its budget allocations negligible. Last year, the Department’s Director General Hubert Mweli told Parliament that a “National Reading Plan” was being implemented by all Provincial Education Departments and a number of other “line functions” within the Department. But, experts on the Reading Panel 2030 have noted that the National Reading Plan had not been published, throwing doubt on whether it even exists We queried the Department, and filed records requests for a copy of the reading plan and the minutes of progress meetings touted by the Department of Parliament last year. To date, DBE’s spokesperson Elijah Mhlanga has not responded and our records request is pending. In last year’s budget vote, the Minister reiterated the importance of “improving reading in the early grades”. But, the only budget line item dedicated to reading for Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) had been allocated R11.1 million, amounting to well below 1 percent of the Department’s annual budget. The DBE’s Primary School Reading Improvement Program (PSRIP) also draws a relatively small budget and its goals and interventions, the panel have concluded, fall well short of what is needed. The lack of a budget for reading is not because the budget is not nuanced. A number of other Department specific priority areas have been allocated conditional grants to which are disbursed directly to provinces, there is no such grant for reading. Indeed, the bulk of the education sector’s budget is spent at the level of provincial departments of education, which run schools and employ teachers. The Reading Panel concluded that most provincial departments have also not planned, developed programs or allocated budgets specifically for improved reading outcomes. Also, a major shortcoming hampering the effective teaching of reading is that teachers and classrooms are not equipped with the physical materials and resources that are needed. In his 2019 SONA, President Ramaphosa said that “[Government] will be substantially expanding the availability of these early reading resources across the foundation phase of schooling”. In 2008, the Department published a list of ten minimum resources needed for literacy teaching, but only DBE “workbooks”, leaving a massive resource gap. Field reporting from the coalface of the literacy crisis Further to this high-level picture, this story will be produced on the ground in the Eastern Cape - the country’s poorest province with a history of poor basic education outcomes . Provincial education departments: We have submitted queries to each provincial education department asking them to outline what reading interventions and budgets they have in place, and to respond to the Reading Panel 2030 finding that there are no such funded programs at the provincial level, except programs in the Western Cape and Gauteng.
